question: At a water pump station test rig, a test slug's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 2t^2 + 2t, where t is the time in seconds after the pump starts. Engineers need the speed gained between t = 0 and t = 4 seconds. That speed applies to a slug with a mass of 4 kilograms. (The pump housing is rated for 240 volts, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the energy this slug carries at that speed, in joules, then subtract 6 from that number. Convert what remains into kilojoules, multiply by 11, and then subtract 1 more. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a magnetic-rail-launcher engineer logs, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 5, after that figure was already multiplied by 9 and increased by 5. Before those adjustments, the value was a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value, in joules, carried by a 33,000 gram sled moving at a speed numerically equal to how sharply a linkage's motion is changing at t = 2 seconds, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = t^3 + 2t^2 for t in seconds since release. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a flywheel-rig technician logs, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying a converted energy figure by 6. That figure, in kilojoules, came from converting an energy value in joules that had first been reduced by 5 and then multiplied by 7. The unreduced energy is what a 20,000 gram flywheel segment carries while moving at a speed equal to the larger of two candidate readings on the calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 8 and multiply together to give 7. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

At a satellite-thruster test bay, an engineer must select 3 nozzles out of 7 identical units on a rack for a burn test. The number of different groups of 3 she could form becomes the acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a thruster housing with a mass of 115,000 grams. Find the push this housing requires, in newtons, then subtract 24 from that number, then multiply what remains by 7. Convert what results into kilonewtons, and then subtract 22 more. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

At a piston test cylinder, a piston's position, in meters, follows s(t) = 5t^3 - 2t^2, where t is the time in seconds after ignition. Engineers need the piston's speed at t = 1 second, and they add 29 to that speed to get the acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a connecting rod with a mass of 138 kilograms. (The cylinder is cooled by 4 liters of oil circulating through it, a detail that plays no role here.) Find the push this rod requires, in newtons, then subtract 30 from that number. Convert what remains into kilonewtons. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

The final number a catapult test crew logs, in kilojoules, is 16 more than an earlier figure, which is itself 4 more than a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value in joules that had already been multiplied by 12. The unmultiplied energy is what an 8,000 gram projectile carries while moving at a speed gained between t = 0 and t = 1 second, given that the projectile's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 5t^2 + 5t over that interval. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

A calibration sheet at a roller-coaster launch bay lists two candidate speed readings, in meters per second, for a test cart: the two numbers add up to 13 and multiply together to give 40. Records confirm the true reading is the smaller of the two. Multiplying that speed by 8 gives the actual launch speed of a cart with a mass of 58,000 grams. Find the energy this cart carries at that speed, in joules, then multiply that number by 5. Convert what results into kilojoules. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a crane-hoist engineer records, in kilonewtons, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 10, and then by 8 more. Before those multiplications, the value was a kilonewton reading converted from a force in newtons that a 61 kilogram hoist arm exerts while undergoing a certain acceleration. That acceleration, in meters per second squared, is how sharply the arm's motion is changing at t = 2 seconds, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = 2t^3 + 5t^2 for t in seconds since the motor engages. (The hoist cable is rated for 6 metric tons, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

The final number a drone-rotor test lab records, in kilojoules, is 10 less than an earlier figure, which is itself 4 less than a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value in joules. That joule value is the energy a 17,000 gram rotor blade carries while moving at a speed that is 21 more than the number of different ways a technician could choose 4 blades out of 6 identical spares on the shelf. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a wind-turbine nacelle test crew logs, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying a converted energy figure by 5, after that figure was already multiplied by 9. Before that, the value was the energy, in joules, carried by a 7 kilogram test mass moving at a speed that is 19 more than the speed gained by a component between t = 1 second and t = 2 seconds, given that the component's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = t^2 + 4t over that interval. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a hydraulic-press bench technician records, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 5. That figure is itself 24 less than a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value, in joules, carried by an 18 kilogram ram head moving at a certain speed. That speed, in meters per second, is how fast the ram is moving at t = 1 second, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = 3t^3 + 5t^2 for t in seconds after the stroke begins. (The press frame stands 2.4 meters tall, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a car-engine test rig reports, in kilojoules, comes from converting an energy value that had first been multiplied by 7. That unmultiplied energy, in joules, is what a 46,000 gram piston assembly carries while moving at a speed that is 3 less than the larger of two candidate readings on a calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 7 and multiply together to give 12. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

At a piston test cylinder, a piston's position, in meters, follows s(t) = 5t^3 - 2t^2, where t is the time in seconds after ignition. Engineers need the piston's speed at t = 2 seconds. That speed applies to a piston with a mass of 18,000 grams. Find the energy this piston carries at that speed, in joules, then multiply that number by 5, then add 8, and then add 6 more. What is the final number, in joules?

The final number a wind turbine nacelle test crew logs, in kilojoules, comes from converting an energy value that had already been multiplied by 3, after being reduced by 10 and increased by 14. Before those adjustments, the value was the energy, in joules, carried by a 58,000 gram calibration mass moving at a speed equal to the greatest length, in centimeters, that divides evenly into both a 195 centimeter cable and a 77 centimeter cable with nothing left over. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a forklift test yard crew records, in kilonewtons, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 8. That figure is itself 26 less than a kilonewton reading converted from a force in newtons that a 124 kilogram test load exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to the number of different groups of 3 pallets a technician could choose from 6 identical pallets on the yard. (The forklift's mast reaches 4.5 meters high, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

The final number a skateboard-ramp test lab logs, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying a converted energy reading by 8. That reading, in joules before conversion, is the energy a 57 kilogram rider model carries while moving at a speed that is 25 more than the smaller of two candidate readings on a calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 8 and multiply together to give 15. (The ramp's guard rail is painted with 2 liters of sealant, a detail that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a magnetic-rail-launcher engineer records, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 8, after that figure was already multiplied by 12 and by 9. Before those multiplications, the value was a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value, in joules, carried by a 27,000 gram sled moving at a speed gained between t = 3 seconds and t = 4 seconds, given that the sled's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 4t^2 + 6t over that interval. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

At a catapult test rig, technicians run 5 successive launch cycles. On cycle k (for k = 1 through 5), the arm adds exactly 2k minus 1 extra units of tension beyond its base setting; adding up the extra tension from all 5 cycles gives a total, which becomes the acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a counterweight with a mass of 87,000 grams. Find the push this counterweight requires, in newtons, then add 2 to that number, then multiply what remains by 11, and then by 6. Convert the result into kilonewtons. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

At a robotic-arm joint test bench, a joint's position, in meters, follows s(t) = t^3 + 3t^2, where t is the time in seconds after actuation. Engineers need the joint's speed at t = 2 seconds. That speed acts as the acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a housing with a mass of 134 kilograms. (The housing's mounting plate is 0.7 meters across, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the push this housing requires, in newtons, then convert that number into kilonewtons. Multiply the result by 6, then by 8, and then add 1 more. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

At a go-kart track test bay, a kart's position along the straightaway, in meters, follows s(t) = t^3 + 2t^2, where t is the time in seconds since the start. Engineers need the kart's speed at t = 2 seconds. That speed applies to a scale-model kart with a mass of 28 kilograms. Find the energy this kart carries at that speed, in joules, then convert that number into kilojoules. Subtract 10 from the result, then multiply what remains by 10, and then by 7. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a forklift test yard crew reports, in kilonewtons, comes from converting a force value in newtons that had first been multiplied by 12, then by 2. The unmultiplied force is what a 147 kilogram test load exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to the speed a linkage reaches at t = 1 second, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = 5t^3 - 3t^2 for t in seconds after actuation. (The forklift's tires are inflated to 90 psi, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

The final number a robotics-lab technician logs, in joules, is 9 less than an earlier figure, which is itself 13 less than an energy reading that had been multiplied by 10. The unmultiplied energy, in joules, is what a 43 kilogram test arm carries while moving at a speed equal to the number of different groups of 3 servo motors a technician could choose from 8 identical units on the shelf. What is the final number, in joules?

The final number a wind turbine nacelle test crew logs, in kilojoules, is 7 less than an earlier figure, which is itself 15 more than a value that was, before that, 29 less than a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value in joules. That joule value is the energy a 4 kilogram calibration mass carries while moving at a speed equal to the larger of two candidate readings on a calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 11 and multiply together to give 24. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

At a car-engine test rig, a piston's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = t^2 + 3t, where t is the time in seconds after ignition. Engineers need the speed gained between t = 1 second and t = 2 seconds, and they add 13 to that speed to get the acceleration of a connecting rod with a mass of 95 kilograms. Find the push this rod requires, in newtons, then convert that number into kilonewtons. Subtract 20 from the result, and then add 15 more. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

The final number a wind-tunnel model test lab logs, in joules, is 10 less than an earlier figure, which is itself 19 more than an energy reading that had been multiplied by 10. The unmultiplied energy, in joules, is what a 45 kilogram scale model carries while moving at a speed gained between t = 0 and t = 1 second, given that the model's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 5t^2 over that interval. (The tunnel's intake fan spins at 1800 rpm, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in joules?
